say: Why did a bank's margin fall when money poured in? In one quarter, Kotak Mahindra Bank took in about fifty five thousand, three hundred and forty four crore rupees of foreign-currency deposits.
That is the bank's own figure. And its release says the fall in the margin was 'largely on account of' those deposits.
Yet profit rose twenty nine percent from a year earlier, to four thousand, two hundred and twelve crore rupees. A thinner margin, a bigger bank, more profit. How does that happen?
So our question: how much of Kotak's growth came from that foreign money, and what did it do to the bank's cheap-money advantage?

First, what is an F C N R deposit? A plain definition, from the Reserve Bank's rules, not the filing: a fixed-term deposit in a foreign currency, held with an Indian bank by an Indian citizen or person of Indian origin living abroad, for one to five years. The filing adds one phrase: 'pursuant to R B I's swap facility'.

How big? Total deposits at the end of September were six lakh, fifty one thousand crore. The foreign deposits were about eight and a half percent of that, by our arithmetic. Yet without them, the bank says, deposits grew thirteen percent over the year, not twenty three.

Loans tell a similar story. Net advances, the loans the bank has given out, grew twenty five percent. Leave out loans against the foreign deposits, and a loan book taken over from its subsidiary, Kotak Mahindra Investments, the bank says, and it is nineteen percent.

The loans against the foreign deposits were about sixteen thousand, one hundred and ten crore. The deck also notes eight thousand, nine hundred and fifteen crore of loans transferred from that subsidiary. The release gives no amounts for what it left out, but taking off both gives about nineteen percent, our arithmetic.

Where did the money go? Between June and September, deposits rose from about five lakh, seventy three thousand crore to six lakh, fifty one thousand. Borrowings more than doubled, to about fifty five thousand crore.

Total assets rose by about one lakh, twelve thousand crore in three months, our arithmetic. Cash and short-term balances rose from about forty five thousand crore to about eighty one thousand, up eighty one percent. The filing does not say that cash is the foreign money.

Now the margin. Net interest margin, or N I M, is, in plain words, what a bank earns on its loans and investments, minus what it pays for money, as a percentage of its earning assets. Kotak's was four point three one percent; a year ago, four point five four; in June, four point five three.

A lower margin is not lower income. Net interest income, the rupees themselves, rose sixteen percent from a year ago, to eight thousand, four hundred and fifty nine crore. A thinner slice, of a bigger pie.
So did money get dearer? Not over the year. Cost of funds, what the bank pays for money, was four point five two percent, against four point seven a year ago, but up from four point four six in June.

Now the cheap-money advantage. Money left in ordinary current and savings accounts, called Kasa, usually costs a bank less than fixed deposits: a plain definition. Its share of deposits fell to thirty eight point two percent from forty two point three a year ago. Did the advantage shrink?
The bank says the fall reflects 'the increase in the term deposit base due to F C N R B deposit inflows'. Leave the foreign deposits out, it says, and the ratio is forty one point eight percent.

We checked. Cheap deposits were two lakh, forty nine thousand crore. Take the foreign deposits out of the total and about five lakh, ninety six thousand crore is left. Divide: forty one point eight percent. The bank's number holds, our arithmetic.
But that is still half a point below a year ago, our arithmetic: on the bank's own adjusted figure, the cheap-money share slipped a little.

So why did profit still rise? Net total income grew eighteen percent, while costs grew fourteen, so operating profit rose twenty one. And credit cost, the yearly bad-loan charge, fell from zero point seven nine percent to zero point three five.

The fee line has a footnote. Fees grew twenty one percent, but include about one hundred and fifty eight crore of processing fees on loans against the foreign deposits. Without them, about fifteen percent, our arithmetic.

One more thing from the same day. The board appointed Anup Kumar Saha, now a whole-time director, as managing director and chief executive for three years from the first of January twenty twenty seven, subject to the members' approval. The R B I approved it on the thirtieth of September.
But. Here is what the filings do not say. What the foreign deposits cost the bank, and how long they run. The terms of the R B I swap facility. And the margin without the foreign money.

So every adjusted number we have given you, thirteen, nineteen, forty one point eight, is the bank's own choice of what to leave out. Our reading: the one adjusted number that would settle the margin question is missing.

Provisions, the money set aside for bad loans, fell fifteen percent overall. But provisions on standard assets, loans not classed as bad, rose to two hundred and seventy four crore, from seventy five a year ago. About one hundred and twenty crore of that is on loans against the foreign deposits and loans transferred from Kotak Mahindra Investments.
Do the international branches only add income? The deck also notes about one hundred and sixteen crore of fees and other costs on money those branches borrowed. The filings do not net it all out.
And there is no outlook: no guidance on margin, loan growth or credit cost in any of the three documents.

The bank's side: it labels each adjusted figure and footnotes the fees itself. Return on equity was eleven point six five percent, against ten point three eight a year ago, but eleven point nine eight in June.

So, back to fifty five thousand, three hundred and forty four crore rupees. The bank says taking it in was largely behind the fall in the margin. Its filings show the deposits and the lower margin. They do not show what that foreign money costs.
The next filing to read is the December quarter: the margin again, and whether the bank gives it without the foreign deposits.
